issues.description: The problem specification and UML require a StockIngredient constructor with signature StockIngredient(String, int, int), and the solution implements this 3-argument constructor. However, the template StockIngredient class only provides a constructor with signature StockIngredient(String, int, int, boolean). This mismatch is structural: students will be instructed (and the UML shows) to use the 3-arg constructor but the template does not provide it, which can cause confusion and compilation friction when following the exercise or when comparing to the solution.
issues.suggestedFix: Provide the 3-argument constructor StockIngredient(String name, int price, int quantity) in the template (either by adding an overload that delegates to the existing constructor or by replacing the 4-arg constructor with the 3-arg version used in the UML). This will align the template with the problem specification and the solution while preserving any intended validation logic.

issues.description: The problem statement and the solution expect a StockIngredient constructor with the signature StockIngredient(String, int, int), but the template's StockIngredient class only provides a constructor StockIngredient(String, int, int, boolean strictValidation). This API/signature mismatch between the template and the expected/solution API creates confusion: students following the problem description or the solution will look for a 3-argument constructor that is not present in the starter code, making it unclear how to instantiate StockIngredient as required by the exercise.
issues.suggestedFix: Modify the template StockIngredient class to include the 3-argument constructor StockIngredient(String name, int price, int quantity) (either by adding an overloaded constructor or replacing the 4-arg constructor), so the template API matches the problem statement and the solution. Alternatively, update the problem statement to document the additional boolean parameter if that was intentional.
